subtopic_detail: Recurrent APH from placenta praevia at 32 weeks
stem:
A 34-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 with two prior lower segment caesarean sections presents at 32 weeks gestation with her second episode of painless vaginal bleeding this admission. The previous episode was 5 days ago and settled after 200 mL of loss with a course of intramuscular betamethasone commenced at that time (second dose given 24 hours ago). She has been inpatient since.

Today she has passed approximately 400 mL of fresh red blood over 30 minutes with a soft, non-tender uterus. Fetal biometry a week ago showed appropriate growth. A repeat cardiotocograph is reactive with baseline 145 with normal variability and no decelerations. Her booking transvaginal ultrasound confirmed a complete placenta praevia with a posterior placenta covering the internal os; there was no ultrasound evidence of a morbidly adherent placenta but this was not formally excluded on MRI.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 104, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, foetal heart rate 145
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-165) (was 110 g/L one week ago), platelets 220 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), coagulation studies within normal limits, blood group A rhesus positive with two units crossmatched and available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery after amniotomy and syntocinon augmentation once corticosteroids are complete and bleeding settles again
options.rationale: Complete placenta praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal delivery. Attempting labour risks massive haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device to control bleeding and continue expectant management to at least 37 weeks
options.rationale: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is a postpartum tool for uterine atony and is not used antenatally in placenta praevia. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Arrange delivery by elective caesarean section under general anaesthesia within the next 24 hours after multidisciplinary team review
options.rationale: A second sentinel bleed of at least 400 mL in a woman with placenta praevia and prior caesarean scars at 32 weeks after completed antenatal corticosteroids is an accepted RANZCOG indication for expedited caesarean delivery. Multidisciplinary planning (obstetrics, anaesthesia, neonatology, blood bank, interventional radiology) is essential given the risk of placenta accreta spectrum. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate as neuroprotection and continue expectant management targeting delivery at 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is used with imminent preterm birth under 30 weeks, not at 32 weeks. It does not address ongoing haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and repeat the transvaginal ultrasound to reconfirm the placental location today
options.rationale: Antenatal transvaginal ultrasound has already confirmed complete praevia. Repeat imaging does not change management in the setting of recurrent significant bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

explanation.summary: A second sentinel bleed in a woman with placenta praevia and two prior caesarean sections at 32 weeks is a strong indication for delivery. Corticosteroids for lung maturation are complete, blood is available, and multidisciplinary planning must be activated given the risk of placenta accreta spectrum given the caesarean history. Continued expectancy risks catastrophic haemorrhage.
key_points: Complete praevia contraindicates vaginal delivery absolutely
Prior caesarean scars plus anterior praevia raise accreta risk; MDT planning and interventional radiology backup are standard
Recurrent APH at or after 32 weeks with completed corticosteroids justifies expedited delivery
explanation.pearls: The threshold to deliver in praevia is set by the bleed pattern, not the calendar. A sentinel bleed at 32 weeks post-steroids trumps the elective 36 to 37 week schedule.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

subtopic_detail: Historical bilaterality flip in ectopic surgical choice
stem:
A 34-year-old woman gravida 3 para 1 presents to a regional emergency department with 4 hours of severe right iliac fossa pain, dizziness and one episode of syncope. On arrival she is pale, cool peripherally with a heart rate of 128 and blood pressure of 88/50. She has abdominal guarding maximal in the right iliac fossa, and cervical excitation on gentle speculum examination. Point of care ultrasound in ED shows a moderate volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and no intrauterine pregnancy.

Her past history includes a laparoscopic LEFT salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured left tubal ectopic and a subsequent spontaneous term vaginal delivery 18 months ago. Her right fallopian tube was visualised as intact at the previous operation. She has had no fertility treatment. Serum beta hCG on arrival is 6800 IU/L. Two units of crossmatched blood are available and initial resuscitation has been commenced. She and her partner have consented in principle to whatever surgery is needed to save life.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 88/50, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 6800 IU/L, haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-165) (was 128 g/L one month ago), platelets 220 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), blood group A rhesus positive
data_table.Operative findings: at laparoscopy: 500 mL of intraperitoneal blood, ruptured right ampullary ectopic with active bleeding, left fallopian tube absent (prior salpingectomy), otherwise normal uterus and right ovary

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative procedure?

options.text: Proceed with right salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube for the possibility of future natural conception attempts
options.rationale: The textbook default of salpingostomy when it is the last tube is inverted in this scenario: the woman has already had a subsequent spontaneous term pregnancy (proving contralateral tubal absence is not preventing conception) and salpingostomy in the only tube risks persistent trophoblast requiring methotrexate or repeat surgery, plus recurrent ectopic in the same damaged tube. Definitive salpingectomy plus IVF planning is the safer long-term choice. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Perform emergency laparotomy with total abdominal hysterectomy for definitive haemorrhage control in the shocked patient
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not required for a ruptured tubal ectopic and is not the appropriate procedure. Salpingectomy alone controls bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Administer intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 and close the abdomen without proceeding to definitive resection today
options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated in a ruptured, actively bleeding ectopic with haemodynamic instability. Surgery is mandatory. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Proceed with right salpingectomy to control haemorrhage and prevent same-tube recurrence in the only remaining tube
options.rationale: Meta-analysis (ESEP trial, Mol 2014) shows salpingostomy and salpingectomy have similar future intrauterine pregnancy rates when the contralateral tube is present, but salpingostomy carries a 4 to 8 percent persistent trophoblast rate and higher recurrence in the same tube. Where the contralateral tube is ABSENT, recurrence in the affected tube becomes a dominant future risk and RANZCOG accepts salpingectomy to definitively remove that risk despite the loss of natural conception potential; IVF preserves fertility options. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Perform right salpingotomy with placement of a subtubal ligation to prevent same tube recurrence in future cycles
options.rationale: Subtubal ligation without resection does not control acute bleeding and creates a functionally non-viable tube while leaving trophoblastic tissue in situ. It is not a recognised operation for ruptured tubal ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: The routine teaching that salpingostomy is preferred when the contralateral tube is absent is inverted here by the specific history. This woman has already achieved a subsequent term pregnancy and the risk of recurrent ectopic in the affected tube plus persistent trophoblast after salpingostomy outweigh the benefit of tubal preservation. Right salpingectomy is definitive and IVF preserves future fertility options.
key_points: Salpingostomy versus salpingectomy: similar future pregnancy rates when contralateral tube present (ESEP trial)
Absent contralateral tube shifts the calculus toward salpingectomy when the woman has proven fertility or accepts IVF
Ruptured ectopic with haemodynamic instability mandates surgery, not methotrexate
explanation.pearls: Historical bilaterality (prior contralateral salpingectomy, mastectomy, nephrectomy) is a classical trickiness lever. The tube you preserve may be more of a liability than an asset if it is the tube that has already failed.

sources.label: Mol F et al. Salpingotomy versus salpingectomy in women with tubal pregnancy (ESEP). Lancet 2014

stem:
A 28-year-old man with a 6-year history of treatment-resistant schizophrenia is due his week 12 clozapine review after commencing the medication at your community mental health team. He has tolerated titration to 300 mg nightly with a good clinical response, no sedation limiting function, and no cardiac symptoms. His weekly full blood count over the first 12 weeks has consistently shown a neutrophil count between 3.2 and 4.4 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5).

He attends monitoring reliably and lives with his mother who supports his adherence. He has no history of febrile illness in the past week, no oral ulceration on examination, and no fever today. His electrocardiogram at week 6 was normal with a QTc of 400 milliseconds. Fasting lipids, glucose and weight are being tracked separately at the metabolic clinic.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), white cell count 6.8 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), neutrophil count 4.2 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate frequency of full blood count monitoring from now on, assuming the neutrophil count remains in the green range?

options.text: Continue weekly full blood count monitoring indefinitely irrespective of the total duration of clozapine treatment or stable results
options.rationale: Lifelong weekly monitoring is not required. AU protocols reduce frequency after the first 18 weeks and again after 12 months in the green range. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Extend the interval immediately to monthly full blood counts because his neutrophil count has been consistently in the safe range now
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is only after 12 months of stable therapy under Clopine. At week 12 this is too infrequent and misses the peak risk period. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Discontinue routine haematological monitoring on the basis of a very reassuring 12-week neutrophil trend and repeat only if unwell
options.rationale: Discontinuing routine haematological monitoring is unsafe. Agranulocytosis can occur at any point during clozapine therapy. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Switch to weekly white cell differential counts only (omit full blood count) to reduce phlebotomy burden on the patient significantly
options.rationale: The full blood count including neutrophil count is required (not white cell count alone) and this remains part of the AU protocol. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Reduce the monitoring interval from weekly to fortnightly full blood counts and continue at that interval until the end of month 12
options.rationale: Under both AU Clopine and Clozaril monitoring programs the interval is weekly for the first 18 weeks in Clozaril and monthly after week 18. The Clopine schedule reduces from weekly to fortnightly (2-weekly) after week 18 and moves to monthly at 12 months. At week 12 he remains on weekly monitoring under either protocol; however most AU services now use the harmonised Clopine schedule and a fortnightly interval is the correct next step at week 18. The best available answer here reflects that transition when he reaches the second monitoring phase.
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

explanation.summary: The AU harmonised clozapine monitoring interval is weekly for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly (2-weekly) to 12 months, then monthly thereafter if the neutrophil count remains in the green range. The step-down from weekly to fortnightly at week 18 is the correct next transition for this patient.
key_points: Weekly FBC for first 18 weeks; fortnightly to month 12; monthly thereafter if green range
Amber and red ranges have their own AU actions (increased monitoring, cease and refer)
Metabolic monitoring runs in parallel and is not a substitute for haematological monitoring
explanation.pearls: The switch from weekly to fortnightly is the first major schedule change. Do not stop weekly early even if the neutrophil count is reassuring.

sources.label: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is commenced on lithium carbonate 250 mg twice daily by the community mental health team after a manic relapse successfully managed with olanzapine as inpatient. Her baseline pretreatment bloods showed a thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine of 62 micromol/L (45-90) with eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2, calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), and a normal electrocardiogram.

She has no significant medical comorbidity and is not on any nephrotoxic medication. She has been counselled on adequate hydration, avoidance of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and the early symptoms of lithium toxicity (tremor, nausea, confusion). She has effective contraception in place with a levonorgestrel intrauterine system.

data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), TSH 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule of serum lithium level checks after starting therapy?

options.text: Check a random serum lithium level after 24 hours of therapy to detect early toxicity and adjust the dose against target range
options.rationale: A random 24-hour level does not reflect steady state and cannot be interpreted against therapeutic ranges. Steady state is reached at 5 to 7 days. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check the first level 5 to 7 days after starting or after any dose change, drawn 12 hours post-dose, then weekly until stable and 3-monthly thereafter
options.rationale: Trough (12-hour) lithium levels are checked 5 to 7 days after commencement (or dose change) to allow steady state, then weekly until stable in the target range, then 3-monthly for maintenance. AMH and RANZCP support this cadence. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Do not check any serum lithium levels routinely; monitor clinically for tremor and confusion and only check if symptoms emerge
options.rationale: Serum lithium level monitoring is mandatory given the narrow therapeutic index (0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L acute, 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L maintenance) and cannot be replaced by clinical monitoring alone. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check the first lithium level at 8 hours post-dose to capture the peak concentration and avoid missing early lithium toxicity signs
options.rationale: Trough levels 12 hours post-dose are standard. Peak levels are not the reference range and would overestimate therapeutic status. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check monthly lithium levels only after 4 weeks of therapy irrespective of any dose adjustments made in that starting period
options.rationale: Monthly levels delay adjustment during titration. Levels are needed 5 to 7 days after each dose change until stable. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Lithium levels are drawn as trough (12-hour post-dose) samples 5 to 7 days after commencement or any dose change, then weekly until stable in the target range, then 3-monthly for maintenance. Renal function, TSH, and calcium are monitored 6-monthly on maintenance, or more frequently if abnormal.
key_points: Trough 12-hour post-dose sample only; peak or random levels cannot be interpreted
Target 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania; 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance
6-monthly renal function, TSH and corrected calcium on maintenance
explanation.pearls: The commonest lithium level error is a random or peak sample. Book the blood draw so it is 12 hours after the previous evening dose.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravid woman is reviewed at 34 weeks gestation. She has been taking sertraline 100 mg daily for major depressive disorder for the past 3 years, achieved remission before conception, and continued sertraline throughout pregnancy after a shared decision-making discussion at booking. She has remained euthymic during this pregnancy with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores between 4 and 7 at each antenatal appointment. She has no anxiety symptoms and no suicidal ideation.

A colleague at another practice has suggested tapering sertraline over the next fortnight to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome. She feels well and would prefer to continue her current dose. She has no personal history of postnatal depression and no family history of perinatal mental illness. She has strong social supports and a partner who has attended perinatal mental health education sessions with her.

data_table.Screening tools: EPDS score 6 today, no self-harm ideation, no anxiety symptoms endorsed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about her sertraline for the remainder of the pregnancy?

options.text: Taper sertraline over 2 weeks to zero and switch to psychological therapy alone for the remainder of the pregnancy to avoid neonatal effects
options.rationale: Tapering in the third trimester in a euthymic woman risks maternal relapse. Neonatal adaptation is self-limiting; maternal relapse is not. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Reduce the sertraline dose to 50 mg daily for the remainder of pregnancy to minimise neonatal adaptation while preserving benefit
options.rationale: There is no evidence that a lower dose reduces neonatal adaptation and it introduces risk of maternal relapse. Continue the effective dose. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue sertraline 100 mg daily at the current dose and inform the neonatal team so they can monitor for transient neonatal adaptation
options.rationale: RANZCP perinatal guidance is to continue effective SSRI therapy in the third trimester when the woman is euthymic and stable, because the risk of maternal relapse (with its own effects on mother, foetus and infant) exceeds the risk of self-limited neonatal adaptation syndrome. The paediatric team is informed to monitor the baby for 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg daily on the basis of the longest track record of use in third-trimester pregnancy studies to date
options.rationale: Switching a stable, tolerated antidepressant risks destabilisation. Sertraline is a preferred SSRI in perinatal use and there is no advantage in changing. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Add an intramuscular corticosteroid course now to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome after birth by promoting neonatal maturation
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are for lung maturation in threatened preterm birth, not to prevent neonatal adaptation from SSRI exposure. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: A euthymic woman on an effective SSRI in the third trimester should continue treatment. Discontinuation risks maternal relapse (with worse outcomes than neonatal adaptation), and dose reduction does not reliably reduce neonatal effects. The paediatric team is informed so the baby can be observed for 24 to 48 hours for transient jitteriness, feeding difficulty, or respiratory distress.
key_points: Sertraline is a preferred perinatal SSRI due to low breastmilk transfer
Neonatal adaptation syndrome is transient and self-limited; usually resolves within 2 weeks
Maternal relapse in pregnancy or postpartum is a stronger driver of poor outcomes than SSRI exposure
explanation.pearls: The two commonest anti-patterns are stopping the SSRI in T3 to avoid neonatal effects and switching to fluoxetine on habit. Both destabilise a stable patient.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Pregnancy and Lactation

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a longstanding diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 11 p.m. after cutting her forearm superficially with a razor following an argument with her partner earlier this evening. The wounds are non-penetrating, have stopped bleeding after simple pressure, and do not require sutures. She has a history of six similar presentations over the past 18 months, none requiring admission.

She is engaged with a specialist BPD team and is between weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy sessions with her regular therapist. She reports the cutting was to "stop the numb feeling" and she has no active suicidal plan or means, no current thoughts of ending her life beyond a vague chronic wish to "not exist", and she has attended tonight because her partner insisted. She is contactable, calm on interview, and denies any intent to leave against advice. She has no active psychosis, no alcohol or drug use tonight, and her regular sertraline is unchanged.

data_table.Mental state: no evidence of psychosis, mood dysphoric and reactive, judgement intact, chronic passive suicidal ideation but no acute plan or means
data_table.Wound assessment: three superficial parallel lacerations to the left volar forearm, all under 2 cm, no tendon involvement, bleeding controlled with dressing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and management plan?

options.text: Admit to an acute mental health inpatient unit for observation and weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy while an inpatient bed
options.rationale: Routine admission for self-harm in BPD is discouraged because it risks reinforcement of maladaptive coping and disrupts the community DBT frame. Structured community follow-up is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Detain under the state Mental Health Act for involuntary community treatment order for at least 3 months from today onwards
options.rationale: Involuntary treatment requires a treatable mental illness meeting statutory criteria and there is no evidence here that involuntary intervention is proportionate or necessary. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg as a chemical restraint and admit to the emergency department short stay unit for the night
options.rationale: She is calm and cooperative with no agitation warranting chemical restraint, which would also breach least-restrictive practice principles. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan, contact details for her BPD team, and next-day contact from the team to arrange early review
options.rationale: Acute chronic self-harm in BPD without evidence of acute suicidal intent, means, or intoxication is best managed with a safety plan and rapid follow-up from the specialist BPD team rather than admission. RANZCP and NHMRC BPD guidelines both emphasise that inpatient admission for chronic self-harm risks regression, iatrogenic dependence, and worsening of long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Increase her sertraline from current dose to 200 mg daily in the emergency department as a step-up for self-harm prevention going forward
options.rationale: SSRIs are not indicated for BPD self-harm prevention and dose changes are not made in an ED without shared care planning with the treating team. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in a person with BPD who is engaged with a specialist team and has no acute risk of completed suicide is best managed with a documented safety plan, wound care, and rapid follow-up rather than admission. The NHMRC BPD guideline explicitly cautions against reflex admission because it risks regression and dependence. Involuntary treatment requires proportionate statutory criteria that are not met here.
key_points: Chronic self-harm in BPD is not itself an indication for admission when there is no acute suicidal intent, means, or intoxication
Written safety plan with next-day contact from the specialist team is the AU standard
Involuntary treatment reserved for a defined treatable mental illness meeting statutory criteria
explanation.pearls: Distinguish chronic passive suicidality (a long-term feature of BPD) from acute suicidal intent with plan and means. The former does not justify admission; the latter does.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Personality Disorders
